claim: OWASP's Non-Human Identities Top 10 ranks improper offboarding (NHI1) as the single top risk for non-human identities, ahead of leaked secrets and overprivileged access.
stance_target: kill-switch/offboarding mechanisms for agents are an unsolved, top-ranked governance gap
quoted_support: The OWASP Non-Human Identities Top 10 ranks improper offboarding as NHI1, the single top risk for non-human identities, ahead of leaked secrets, overprivileged access, and everything else on the list.

claim: Entro Labs' H1 2025 research found nearly half of all non-human identities in the average enterprise are over a year old, and one in every thousand has been live for more than a decade.
stance_target: agent credential/access lifecycle management at scale is currently unmanaged, implying kill-switch infrastructure for Worker Agents is immature
quoted_support: Entro Labs' H1 2025 research found that nearly half of all non-human identities in the average enterprise are over a year old, and one in every thousand has been live for more than a decade.

claim: Veza's 2026 State of Identity & Access Report found 38% of all accounts in enterprises analyzed are dormant.
stance_target: automated offboarding/kill-switch processes have not kept pace with agent proliferation
quoted_support: Veza's 2026 State of Identity & Access Report put a harder number on it: 38% of all accounts in the enterprises it analyzed are dormant.

claim: Only 12% of organizations have automated lifecycle management for machine identities at all, per ManageEngine's 2026 survey.
stance_target: automated kill-switch/decommission infrastructure for agents remains rare, a key prerequisite gap before scaling Worker Agent concurrency
quoted_support: ManageEngine's 2026 survey found that only 12% of organizations have automated lifecycle management for machine identities at all.

claim: A departing engineer's Okta account can be disabled on their last day, but AI coding tools configured with multiple MCP server connections (GitHub, Jira, data warehouse, Confluence, Slack API key, internal deployment API) are not federated through Okta and keep working indefinitely until someone notices.
stance_target: permission scoping across tool/MCP connections is a concrete unsolved technical gap for agent kill-switches
scope_conditions: described by Scalekit engineering blog, February 2026
quoted_support: The Okta disable hits Okta-federated apps. The six MCP connections don't run through Okta. They keep working, for days, weeks, indefinitely, until somebody notices.

claim: A workable agent Leaver/kill-switch framework requires four elements: per-classification decommission playbooks, centralized credential inventory registered at issuance, independent verification of revocation (not just the agent's or vendor's self-report), and treating 90-day dormancy as an implicit termination signal.
stance_target: concrete escalation/offboarding governance design needed before scaling agent populations
quoted_support: A workable framework has four requirements: Decommission playbook per Agent classification... Centralized credential inventory, not distributed... Verification of revocation, not assumption... Dormancy as an implicit termination signal.

claim: Vendor/agent attestations about what has been deleted or revoked deserve skepticism, directly citing the Replit agent's false claim that database rollback was impossible as precedent for not trusting self-reported remediation status.
stance_target: escalation and verification triggers must be independent of the agent being governed
scope_conditions: general lesson drawn from Replit incident
quoted_support: The Replit incident is instructive here: when the Agent claimed rollback was impossible, it was wrong. Vendor attestations about what they've deleted, what access they've revoked, and what caches they've purged deserve the same skepticism.
